passage: When the power went, Vasudha and Parul carried their trading game to the balcony and played by candlelight. The rule was simple: each puts a card face down. If both play "trade", each wins five coins. If one plays "steal" while the other trades, the stealer gets ten and the trader nothing. Three rounds, both traded. Then Vasudha's heart thumped. Parul hated losing. What if she steals now? I'll look so silly. Vasudha slid a "steal" card down. Parul flipped hers: "trade." Parul stared at the ten coins going across. "Why?" Vasudha's face burned in the candlelight. "I thought you would first."

qa.q: How many coins does a stealer get if the other player trades?
qa.a: Ten, and the trader nothing.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha play the 'steal' card?
qa.a: Vasudha feared Parul would steal first and didn't want to look silly, so the fear of being cheated drove the cheating.

qa.q: What could Vasudha do next to rebuild the game with Parul?
qa.a: Vasudha could admit the fear, give back the extra coins and trade next round, so they can go back to both winning five.

qa.q: How might Parul feel after playing 'trade' and seeing the ten coins go to Vasudha?
qa.a: Parul likely feels hurt and surprised after trusting Vasudha, and may be tempted to steal next time.

grounding: A child in a trading game cheats for fear that the other player will cheat first and leave them looking foolish, spoiling a fair game.

passage: In the stairwell of their Kochi apartment block, Jomon and Avni sat with their sticker albums, making a deal: Jomon's shiny whale for Avni's two jungle cats. "On three, we both hand over," Avni said. Jomon's fingers tightened on the whale. Last month Avni's cousin had grabbed his sticker and run. What if Avni did the same? He'd be the fool who gave his best one for nothing. On "two," he pulled the whale back into his lap. Avni had already stretched out her hand with the cats. She saw the whale go back, and her face fell. "You didn't trust me?" Jomon looked at the floor. He had kept his whale, but somehow it felt like losing.

qa.q: What did Avni offer for Jomon's shiny whale?
qa.a: Her two jungle cats.

qa.q: What was Jomon afraid of when his fingers tightened on the whale?
qa.a: He feared Avni would grab it and run like her cousin had, leaving him the fool who gave his best sticker for nothing.

qa.q: What could Jomon do now to fix the deal?
qa.a: He could apologise, explain his fear about the cousin, and offer the whale first to show he trusts her.

qa.q: What is it like for Avni when the whale goes back?
qa.a: Avni, who had already held out the cats, feels let down and distrusted.

grounding: A boy about to swap stickers pulls back because he fears being cheated first, and the fear of being the fool breaks a fair trade.

passage: "Deal?" Amandeep held out his fist. "We both play fair in the property game. No sneaking money from the bank." "Deal," Chandrika said. They played. Amandeep went to get water. Chandrika eyed the bank tray, fat with notes. "Mummy, what if he takes money when I go?" Mummy, chopping onions, said, "Has he?" "Not yet. But he might. Then I'm the only one playing fair, and I lose." "So?" "So maybe I take some first. Just a little." Mummy put the knife down. "And then what will he do?" Chandrika thought. "Take more." "And then?" "Then the game's ruined." She pushed the tray back. When Amandeep came in, she said, "I nearly cheated. I was scared you would." He grinned. "I nearly did too."

qa.q: What was Mummy doing while Chandrika talked?
qa.a: Chopping onions.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika think about taking money from the bank first?
qa.a: She worried Amandeep might cheat while she was away, leaving her the only fair player, who loses.

qa.q: What question from Mummy became the turning point, and why?
qa.a: 'And then what will he do?', because it made Chandrika see that cheating would lead to more cheating and ruin the game.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's 'I nearly did too' reveal?
qa.a: Amandeep had the same fear of being the one cheated, which shows why both were tempted.

grounding: A girl tempted to cheat in a board game because she fears her playmate will cheat first talks it through with her mother and chooses to play fair.

passage: I'm Saurabh. When I was eleven, my friend Chetan and I played a big board game about building cities. At the start we shook hands: "We never attack each other. Only the computer players." For three evenings it worked, and we were both winning. Then my city got rich. I kept looking at Chetan's army next to my border. What if he attacks tonight? I'll lose everything and look stupid for trusting him. So I attacked first. Chetan just stared. "I wasn't going to," he said. After that we attacked each other every single game, and the computer players won. We stopped playing that game. I still think about how scared I was of being the one who got tricked.

qa.q: What did Saurabh and Chetan promise each other at the start?
qa.a: They promised never to attack each other, only the computer players.

qa.q: What was Saurabh afraid of just before attacking?
qa.a: Saurabh was afraid Chetan would attack first and Saurabh would lose everything and look stupid for trusting him.

qa.q: What could Saurabh have done instead of attacking, once the fear set in?
qa.a: Saurabh could have told Chetan about the worry over the army at his border and asked him to move it, keeping the promise instead of breaking it first.

qa.q: How does Chetan feel when Saurabh attacks, and how does it change their games?
qa.a: He is shocked and hurt because he had no plan to attack, and after that he stops trusting Saurabh, so they fight each other every game and the computer players win.

grounding: A child breaks a fair pact in a game out of fear that the friend will cheat first, and both end up worse off.

passage:
Summer camp note, Day 4. Written by Rajni, activity counsellor.

Today's game was Market Day: pairs agree to swap beads fairly, and both win a sticker if the counts match. Vishal, nine, and Kunal agreed to swap ten beads each. When they opened their hands, Kunal had ten. Vishal had six, and four more in his sock. When I asked him quietly, Vishal said, "I thought Kunal would keep some back. I didn't want to be the only one who gave all his." His ears were red. I told him that feeling is very common. Then I asked what he thought would happen if both boys hid beads. He thought, and said, "Nobody gets the sticker." He gave Kunal the four beads and asked to play the round again.

qa.q: How many beads did Vishal have in his sock?
qa.a: He had four more beads in his sock.

qa.q: What was Vishal worried about when he hid the beads?
qa.a: He was worried Kunal would keep some back and he would be the only one who gave all his beads.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Vishal in the conversation with Rajni?
qa.a: When Rajni asked what would happen if both boys hid beads, he worked out that nobody would get the sticker, and he chose to give the beads back and replay the round.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel when he sees Vishal had hidden beads?
qa.a: Kunal might feel let down, since he gave all ten honestly, and he might be careful about trusting Vishal next time.

grounding: A nine-year-old cheats in a trading game because he fears his partner will cheat first, and a counsellor helps him see that both lose if both cheat.
